Financial Goal Setting: A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound
A financial target reached within about a year
A financial target taking several years or more
Something you own that has value
Money you owe to someone else
A written strategy for reaching your money goals
What you give up by choosing one purchase over another
Passing up a smaller reward now for a larger one later
Directing money toward what actually matters to you
Income and Careers: Take-home pay after taxes and deductions
Fixed annual pay, not tied to hours worked
Extra pay, often time and a half, for hours beyond the standard week
Pay based on a percentage of sales made
Non-wage compensation such as health insurance or retirement matching
The form telling an employer how much tax to withhold
A self-employed worker responsible for their own taxes
How much money is needed to cover basic expenses in an area
Taxes: Income tax
A tax on money earned from work and investments
Withholding
Tax an employer removes from each paycheck and sends to the government
W-2 form
The annual statement of wages and taxes withheld
Tax deduction
An expense that reduces the income you are taxed on
Tax credit
An amount subtracted directly from taxes owed, worth more than a deduction
Standard deduction
A flat amount most filers subtract instead of itemising
Tax bracket
An income range taxed at a particular rate
Marginal tax rate
The rate applied to your next dollar of income, not to all of it
Tax refund
Money returned when you paid more during the year than you owed
FICA
Payroll taxes funding Social Security and Medicare
Sales tax
A tax added at purchase, charged as a percentage of price
Property tax
An annual tax on real estate, usually funding local services
Budgeting and Money Management: Budget
A plan matching income against planned spending and saving
Fixed expense
A cost that stays the same each period, such as rent
Variable expense
A cost that changes each period, such as groceries
Discretionary spending
Optional purchases that are wants rather than needs
A guideline of 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt payoff
Cash flow
The movement of money in and out over a period
Zero-based budget
Assigning every dollar of income a specific job
Overspending
Spending more than income, usually financed by debt
Expense tracking
Recording what you actually spend to compare against the plan
Sinking fund
Saving a set amount monthly toward a known future expense
Banking Services: Checking account
An account for everyday spending with easy access to funds
Savings account
An interest-bearing account for money you do not need immediately
Debit card
A card drawing directly from your bank balance
Direct deposit
Having pay sent electronically into your account
Overdraft
Spending more than your balance, usually triggering a fee
Annual percentage yield
The yearly rate earned on savings, including compounding
Certificate of deposit
A savings product paying more interest if you leave money untouched
Credit union
A member-owned nonprofit alternative to a commercial bank
Routing number
The number identifying your bank in a transfer
Reconciling an account
Comparing your records to the bank statement to catch errors
Credit and Debt: Credit
Borrowing money now with a promise to repay later
Credit card
A revolving line of credit you borrow against and repay monthly
Annual percentage rate
The yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and fees
Minimum payment
The smallest amount you can pay to stay current, which maximises interest paid
Revolving credit
Credit you can reuse as you repay, like a credit card
Installment loan
A loan repaid in fixed payments over a set term
Secured debt
Debt backed by collateral the lender can seize
Unsecured debt
Debt with no collateral, usually carrying higher interest
Debt-to-income ratio
Monthly debt payments as a share of monthly income
Avalanche method
Paying off the highest interest rate debt first to minimise total cost
Snowball method
Paying off the smallest balance first to build momentum
Predatory lending
Loans with abusive terms targeting borrowers with few options
Credit Scores and Reports: Credit score
A number, commonly 300 to 850, summarising credit risk
Credit report
A detailed record of your borrowing and repayment history
Payment history
Whether you pay on time, the largest factor in a credit score
Credit utilization
The share of your available credit you are using
Length of credit history
How long your accounts have been open, which helps your score
Hard inquiry
A lender checking your credit for an application, which can lower your score
Soft inquiry
A credit check that does not affect your score
Credit bureau
A company compiling credit reports, such as Equifax or Experian
Identity theft
Someone using your personal information to open credit in your name
Credit freeze
Blocking new credit in your name to prevent fraud
Saving and Investing: Compound interest
Earning interest on your interest as well as your principal
Rule of 72
Dividing 72 by the interest rate estimates years to double your money
Principal
The original amount saved or invested
Liquidity
How quickly an asset can be turned into cash without losing value
Inflation risk
The danger that rising prices erode the value of your savings
Time horizon
How long until you need the money, which shapes how you invest
Simple interest
Interest calculated only on the original principal
Return on investment
The gain or loss on an investment as a percentage
Dollar-cost averaging
Investing a fixed amount regularly regardless of price
Emergency fund
Three to six months of expenses set aside for the unexpected
Stocks, Bonds, and Mutual Funds: Stock
A share of ownership in a company
Bond
A loan to a company or government that pays interest
Mutual fund
A pooled investment holding many securities, managed professionally
Index fund
A fund tracking a market index, usually with very low fees
ETF
An exchange-traded fund that trades like a stock
Diversification
Spreading money across investments so one loss cannot sink you
Portfolio
The full collection of investments a person holds
Capital gain
Profit from selling an investment for more than you paid
Bull market
A period of generally rising prices
Bear market
A period of generally falling prices
Expense ratio
The annual percentage a fund charges to manage your money
Risk tolerance
How much volatility you can accept without panic selling
Insurance and Risk Management: Paying a premium to transfer the risk of a large loss
The regular payment made to keep an insurance policy active
What you pay out of pocket before insurance begins covering costs
A fixed amount you pay for a covered service
Coverage for vehicle damage and liability to others
The part of a policy paying for harm you cause to others
Inexpensive coverage protecting belongings in a rented home
Coverage paying dependents if the insured person dies
A formal request for an insurer to pay for a covered loss
Housing Decisions: Lease
A binding contract to rent for a set period
Security deposit
Money held by a landlord against damage or unpaid rent
Mortgage
A long-term loan used to buy property, secured by that property
Down payment
Cash paid upfront when buying, reducing the amount financed
Fixed-rate mortgage
A home loan whose interest rate never changes
Adjustable-rate mortgage
A home loan whose rate can rise after an introductory period
Equity in a home
The share of the property's value you actually own
Closing costs
Fees paid at the completion of a property purchase
Foreclosure
The lender seizing a home after the borrower defaults
Renting versus buying
The trade-off between flexibility and building equity
Retirement and Estate Planning: An employer-sponsored retirement account, often with matching contributions
Employer match
Money an employer adds to your retirement account, effectively free pay
IRA
An individual retirement account with tax advantages
Roth IRA
A retirement account funded after tax, with tax-free qualified withdrawals
Traditional IRA
A retirement account funded pre-tax, taxed when withdrawn
Vesting
Earning full ownership of employer contributions over time
Social Security
Federal retirement and disability income funded by payroll taxes
Pension
An employer-funded plan paying a set retirement income
Will
A legal document directing how your property is distributed after death
Beneficiary
The person designated to receive an account or policy payout
